title: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines sensitize tumours to immune checkpoint blockade
one_line: Combines mouse tumour experiments with a retrospective analysis of cancer patients on immune checkpoint blockade to argue that non-tumour-specific SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination acts as a systemic immune stimulant that sensitises tumours to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy.
key_claims: An off-the-shelf mRNA vaccine with no tumour antigen improved responses to checkpoint blockade in mouse tumour models, indicating the effect is adjuvant-like rather than antigen-specific.

The proposed mechanism is systemic type I interferon-driven innate activation that increases intratumoural antigen presentation and PD-L1 expression, converting immunologically 'cold' tumours into checkpoint-responsive ones.

In a retrospective patient cohort, receipt of a SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine close to the start of checkpoint inhibitor therapy was associated with longer overall survival compared with unvaccinated patients on the same therapy.
The benefit was reported in tumour types where checkpoint blockade alone often fails, supporting sensitisation rather than simple additive effect.
The authors frame this as a rationale for cheap, widely available mRNA formulations as universal ICB adjuvants, independent of patient-specific neoantigen design.
limitations: The human evidence is retrospective and observational, so vaccinated patients may differ systematically from unvaccinated ones (healthier, better access to care) despite adjustment.
No prospective randomised trial tested vaccination timing, dose, or formulation against checkpoint blockade alone.
Mouse tumour models may overstate the magnitude of interferon-driven sensitisation seen in humans.
Mechanistic attribution to type I interferon and PD-L1 induction was largely inferred from preclinical systems rather than demonstrated in the patient cohort.
Duration of the sensitised window, and whether repeated vaccination sustains or exhausts it, was not established.
open_questions: A prospective randomised trial of mRNA vaccination timed to checkpoint inhibitor initiation, with overall survival as the endpoint, would settle the central claim.
Does the effect require the lipid nanoparticle/mRNA platform specifically, or would any strong systemic innate stimulus work equally well?
Do paired pre/post tumour biopsies in vaccinated patients show the predicted interferon signature and PD-L1 induction?
What is the optimal interval between vaccination and checkpoint blockade, and does chronic or repeated dosing blunt the benefit?
